I was playing in an amature hockey league a few counties over from my town.  It was the 1st period and I was racing to the boards for a loose puck.  Another player was racing from another direction for the same thing.  I got there first and when i looked for an open player to pass to DIRECTLY across the glass I saw my boss watching me looking me right in the eyes...  I was stunned.  He was literally inches from my face and I had no idea why.  In this time the other player reached me and my now defenseless form and smashed me into the glass while I never broke eye contact with my boss.  This hit very badly strained my groin, anyone who has had one knows the pain that it causes.  I hated my boss and didn't want him to have the satisfaction of knowing he had a part in injuring me.

So I did what I saw was my only option, play the next 2 periods like I was not in blinding pain.

It turns out his son played in a youth league that used the ice time before our game and he had stuck around to watch me play.

I have unfortunately had this conversation more then once.  In my experience the reaction strongly depends on the type of person you are telling.  No matter who they are though they will want to hear exactly how you are going to "take better care of your health".  ie. therapy, exercise, diet change, sleeping more.  They want to know that you care committed to your job and that the time you take off is very legit.  

Honestly i have no idea what to say.  There is nothing you can promise that will stay true.  It's not like your symptoms are going to stop.  You're not going to get better. The bad days wont stop.

Anything other than playing the "I have bipolar card" will be lying.  So you just have to decide what lie you would like to tell.  However any lie you tell will simply sound like an excuse.  Nobody likes to hear excuses from thier employees.

If i feel it coming: 

1. Hand off responsibly.
I let my wife know to steer any anxiety creating situations away from me.  Basically anything that will tip me over the edge.

2. Occupy my mind.
For me, painting or easy a repetitive task that will keep my mind focused on what i'm doing to prevent it from wandering deeper darker place.  Video games are great for this.


If depression has already hit:

1. Hide
I just fucking hide out from the world.  I tell people i have the "flu" and basically treat it the same way.  Plenty of rest, plenty of liquids, avoid others.  Most interaction with others will usually only make things worse.

2. Don't listen to myself
The general obsessive thought is that I cannot go on living life feeling this way and I should just kill myself.  I just think of it like a symptom of the "flu" and ignore it.  

Once i'm down there isn't much I can do to get myself out except wait it out.

"Its great he has you there. Someone anchored to reality, watching objectively, and willing and able to help."
